Understanding and Responding to Online Abuse in Sport
content.paragraph_1: Building Safer Digital Spaces in Sport

content.heading: Building Safer Digital Spaces in Sport
content.paragraph_1: This course from United Against Online Abuse (UAOA) provides practical knowledge and tools to help you recognise online abuse, understand its impact, navigate reporting procedures, and take informed action within your sporting community.

content.heading: About the course
content.paragraph_1:
Course duration

Approximately 90 minutes, completed at your own pace.


Who is it for?

Anyone who participates in, works in, or engages with sport and wants to better understand and respond to online abuse, including athletes, coaches, officials, staff, volunteers, administrators, media professionals, fans, and others across the sporting community.


What can you expect?

Five short modules combine practical guidance, scenarios, and opportunities to apply what you learn. No prior knowledge of online abuse is required.

content.heading: What you’ll explore
content.paragraph_1:
Module 1 · Understanding Online Abuse

Learn to recognise different forms of online abuse, how they can overlap and escalate, and what groups of people face disproportionate risk.


Module 2 · Online Abuse in Sport: The Human Impact

Explore how online abuse can affect athletes with consequences for wellbeing, performance, participation, and sporting communities.

Module 3 · How Online Harm Spreads

Understand how digital platforms, online behaviours, and emerging technologies can amplify harmful content and influence how abuse develops and spreads.

Module 4 · Knowing Your Rights and Responsibilities

Build awareness of your rights, responsibilities, and available reporting pathways, including the roles of platforms, sporting organisations, and other relevant bodies.

Module 5 · Take Action: Building Safer Digital Sport Communities

Turn knowledge into action by exploring practical ways to prevent, respond to, and challenge online abuse within your sporting community.

content.heading: Welcome: Thanks for joining the UAOA mission!
content.paragraph_1: Introduce your topic here. Explain the key ideas and add examples to help learners understand them.

Sport connects millions of people across countries, cultures, and generations through passion, pride, and the thrill of competition.

Online abuse puts that connection at risk. When athletes, officials, volunteers, and fans are attacked online for who they are or how they perform, the consequences can extend far beyond the screen - hurting people, derailing careers, and normalizing abusive behaviour.

United Against Online Abuse (UAOA) brings together more than 75 governments, sports, academics and and technology platforms around a shared goal: making sport safer from online abuse. Lasting change requires action across institutions, communities, and individuals, and that includes you.

Developed in collaboration with the University of Notre Dame, with this eLearning Course, the main goal of the UAOA initiative is to help you to recognise different forms of online abuse, understand their impact on your sporting community, and use reporting procedures with confidence. Once completed, this Course will prepare you to take informed action and contribute to a safer sporting environment.

Thank you for joining the effort.

content.heading: Build your readiness to act
content.paragraph_1:
Awareness is only the beginning. This course builds the practical knowledge and skills needed to understand online abuse and take informed action for yourself and for your sporting community.

The course is designed to meet you wherever you are in your understanding of the topic:

  • If you are already familiar with online abuse, deepen your understanding of reporting systems, digital platforms, AI, and emerging approaches to prevention and response.

  • If the topic is new to you, build a strong foundation and identify practical ways to contribute to safer online practices and digital spaces in sport.

By the end of the course, you will be better equipped to recognise online abuse, respond with confidence, and play an active role in creating safer sport.

content.heading: What do we understand by online abuse?
content.paragraph_1:
Online abuse is any harmful behaviour directed at a person or group through digital platforms.

Definitions vary across countries and contexts, so we focus on what matters most: recognising the harm and building the knowledge to prevent it in sport.

content.paragraph_1:
Online abuse does not affect everyone equally. Some people face more frequent or targeted abuse when hostility focuses on personal characteristics that are considered protected. 

Protected characteristics can include race, ethnicity, nationality, religion, gender, sexual orientation, disability, age, pregnancy status, and marital status.

This list is not exhaustive, and recognised or protected characteristics may vary across legal systems, languages, cultures, and countries. When hostile or malicious language targets someone based on these or other protected characteristics, it may constitute hate speech.

content.heading: When the behaviours overlap:
content.paragraph_1:
Imagine a player receives a humiliating comment after a loss. Similar messages then flood their account for days. Some also attack their race.

The humiliating language is offensive speech. The repeated public aggression in one or across social media platforms creates digital hostility. The racist targeting is considered hate speech.

To recognise what is happening, look at the language, who or what it targets, and the pattern of interactions. More than one behaviour may be present.

content.html:
Key Takeaways

  • Online abuse takes different forms. Offensive speech, hate speech, and digital hostility help us recognise different ways harmful behaviour can appear and develop online.
  • Context matters. Consider the language being used, who or what is being targeted, and the pattern of interactions when identifying online abuse.
  • Different forms of abuse can overlap. A single interaction may involve more than one behaviour, and its characteristics can change as the situation develops.
  • Online abuse can escalate. A single harmful post can develop into repeated or collective hostility as others comment, share, repost, or amplify the content.
  • Some people face disproportionate risk. Identity, visibility, role, and other contextual factors can affect who is targeted and the nature or intensity of the abuse they experience.
  • Recognition is the first step towards action. Understanding what online abuse looks like helps people identify harmful situations and respond more effectively.

content.title: Module 2 - Online Abuse in Sport: The Human Impact
content.subtitle: Estimated time: 15 minutes

content.heading: Why the human impact matters
content.paragraph_1:
Understanding how online abuse affects people helps us build empathy for those targeted and respond with care and respect. The effects of online abuse on people can be serious and far-reaching: a single post can leave someone feeling anxious, unsafe, or doubting themselves even long after the initial interaction.

As abuse continues or spreads across digital platforms, its impact can intensify. Online abuse can affect mental health and wellbeing, as well as how athletes perform, how officials approach decisions, and how journalists and other professionals engage with their work.

Such effects can also extend beyond the person being targeted. Families, teammates, colleagues, and fans may witness or experience the consequences of abuse. At a wider level, persistent online hostility can shape sporting culture, affect participation, and influence who feels safe and welcome in sport.

content.heading: The wider picture
content.paragraph_1:
The effects of online abuse can extend beyond individuals, shaping the culture of sport and the communities around it. Widespread hostility can affect who feels welcome, safe, and able to participate, with implications for inclusion and the sustainability of sporting communities.

Sport also has a wider social influence. The behaviours and attitudes expressed in sporting spaces can contribute to broader social norms. When discriminatory or abusive behaviour becomes normalised, it can reinforce prejudice, exclusion, and hostility beyond sport.

To learn more about the impact and harms of online abuse, we invite you to explore the findings of UAOA’s landmark study captured in please read the UAOA Barometer 2025 - which measures online abuse in sport, with participation from leading NGOs and International Federations.

content.html:
Key Takeaways

  • Online abuse can have wide-ranging effects. Its impact can extend across wellbeing, confidence, sense of safety, performance, participation, and other areas of a person’s life.
  • The effects can be interconnected. Emotional distress, disrupted sleep, reduced confidence, safety concerns, and difficulties with focus can overlap and influence one another.
  • People can be affected differently. Personal and contextual factors can shape how someone experiences and responds to online abuse.
  • The impact extends beyond those directly targeted. Families, teammates, colleagues, fans, organisations, and others across sporting communities can also experience its consequences.
  • Online abuse can affect participation and sporting culture. Persistent hostility can influence who feels safe, welcome, and able to participate in sport.
  • The consequences can extend beyond sport. When discriminatory and abusive behaviours become normalised, they can reinforce prejudice, exclusion, and hostility in wider society.

content.paragraph_1:
Online abuse can spread quickly and reach audiences far beyond the people involved in the original interaction. Digital platforms, user behaviour, and algorithmic systems all influence what content people see and how widely it travels.

Understanding these mechanisms helps us recognise how harmful content can be amplified, how online environments can reinforce hostility, and where opportunities exist to interrupt its spread. The same platforms and technologies that can amplify harmful content can also support its detection, moderation, and prevention.

content.heading: How platforms help reduce online abuse
content.paragraph_1:
Platforms act as intermediaries between people, content, and communities. Their design can influence the reach of harmful content, and their built-in tools can also help detect, limit, report, and respond to abuse.

These measures can include content moderation, reduced distribution of harmful content, prompts before posting, user safety settings, reporting mechanisms, and community standards. Regulation is also increasingly shaping platform responsibilities. 

In most countries of the world, these platforms have a fiduciary duty (in the UK, for example, the Online Safety Act and in Europe, the Digital Services Act) to assess risks, protect users from illegal content, provide reporting mechanisms, and implement proportionate safety measures.

content.heading: AI and Online Harm
content.paragraph_1: AI is changing how online harm can be created and how it is shared. But AI can also be a powerful tool to avoid unwanted content spreading online.

content.html:
Potential risks

  • Creating and amplifying harm: Generative AI can produce or manipulate text, images, audio, and video quickly and at scale.

Potential benefits

  • Detecting harmful content: AI can help identify potentially harmful content and patterns across large volumes of online activity.
  • Supporting moderation: Automated systems can flag content for review and help moderators prioritise potential risks.
  • Supporting users: AI-enabled tools can help filter unwanted content and connect people with reporting and safety features.

content.html:
Key Takeaways

  • Platform design influences how content spreads. Different digital environments shape who encounters content, how people interact with it, and how long it remains visible.
  • Online harm can be amplified. Recommendation systems, sharing, live interaction, and community dynamics can increase the reach and intensity of harmful content.
  • Abusive tactics can adapt. Harmful content may use altered language, visual formats, indirect targeting, or different digital spaces to make detection more difficult.
  • People can take steps to reduce exposure. Privacy controls, interaction settings, blocking, muting, and thoughtful choices about online spaces can support digital wellbeing.
  • Effective reporting follows a clear process. Assess the situation, document relevant evidence, report through an appropriate channel, and seek support or escalate when safety is at risk.
  • AI has a dual role. It can increase the scale and sophistication of harmful content, and it can also support detection, moderation, and other online safety measures.
  • Technology alone cannot address online abuse. Effective responses combine platform tools, responsible user behaviour, human judgement, organisational support, and appropriate regulation.

content.title: Module 4 - Knowing Your Rights and Responsibilities
content.subtitle: Estimated time: 15 minutes

content.heading:
When online abuse occurs, important questions can arise: Is there a law which can help? Who can take action? What other protections are available?
The answers depend on the behaviour, where it occurs, and the laws that can help. Understanding the main legal pathways can help you recognise where legal accountability may be possible and when other forms of action are important.
In sport, legal protections work alongside organisational policies, codes of conduct, safeguarding procedures, and standards of sportsmanship. Together, these mechanisms help establish expectations for safer participation online.

content.heading: Three legal pathways
content.paragraph_1:
Online abuse may engage criminal, civil, or administrative law and regulations. Each pathway involves different actors, processes, and potential outcomes, and the same incident may involve more than one.

These pathways are not mutually exclusive. The same incident may raise different legal issues depending on what occurred and which laws apply.

content.heading: Responsibilities beyond the law
content.paragraph_1:
The law establishes legal obligations. Sport also establishes standards for participation and conduct.

Codes of conduct, safeguarding procedures, safety policies, disciplinary processes, and community standards can help sporting organisations respond to harmful behaviour even when a legal pathway is unavailable or inappropriate.

content.heading: Who can do what
content.paragraph_1:
Sporting organisations should:

  • Define online abuse and expected online conduct codes in organisational policies

  • Establish clear and accessible reporting procedures

  • Apply organisational consequences when codes of conduct are breached

  • Provide education on recognising, preventing, and responding to online abuse

  • Provide access to welfare and safeguarding support

  • Cooperate with platforms, regulators, or relevant authorities where appropriate
content.paragraph_2:
Everyone in sport should:

  • Follow the codes of conduct and policies associated with their role

  • Use appropriate channels to report harmful behaviour

  • Avoid sharing or amplifying abusive content

  • Support people who are targeted

  • Recognise that standards of respect, fair play, and sportsmanship also apply in digital spaces

content.paragraph_1: International federations, national governing bodies, clubs, leagues, and other sporting organisations may have different responsibilities and resources. Clear policies and consistent processes help translate shared standards into action across different levels of sport.

content.html:
Key Takeaways

  • Online abuse can engage different areas of law. Criminal, civil, and administrative pathways involve different processes, actors, and possible outcomes.
  • More than one pathway may apply. The same incident can raise criminal, civil, or regulatory issues depending on the circumstances.
  • Legal responses depend on context and jurisdiction. The applicable law, available evidence, and location of the people and services involved can affect what action is possible.
  • Legal pathways have practical limits. Cross-border activity, identifying responsible individuals, enforcement capacity, and legal thresholds can make action difficult.
  • Responsibility extends beyond the law. Sporting organisations can establish policies, reporting procedures, safeguarding support, and consequences for harmful behaviour.
  • Sportsmanship extends to digital spaces. Respect, fair play, and responsible conduct remain relevant when people participate in sport online.

content.title: Module 5 - Take Action: Building Safer Digital Sport Communities
content.subtitle: Estimated time: 15 minutes

content.heading:
Online abuse in sport can affect one person directly, but no one has to respond to it alone. We can each play a part in creating safer digital spaces, whether we are protecting our own wellbeing, supporting someone who is being targeted, witnessing harmful behaviour, or helping others through our work in sport.

The actions we can take depend on our role and circumstances. Individuals can protect themselves and support others. Organisations can provide clear pathways for reporting, support, and coordinated action. Across sporting communities, education, research, policy, and shared standards can help prevent harm and strengthen how we respond.

In this final module, you will explore how these different levels of action connect, where you can contribute, and how working together can help build safer digital sporting communities.

content.html:
Key Takeaways

  • Tackling online abuse is a shared responsibility. Individuals, sport organisations, platforms, media, advocacy groups, policymakers, and other stakeholders each have a role in prevention and response.
  • Individual actions can reduce harm. Managing exposure, using safety tools, preserving evidence, supporting others, and knowing when to seek additional help can protect safety and wellbeing.
  • Organisations provide structure and support. Clear frameworks, safeguarding, reporting pathways, and coordinated action help organisations prepare for and respond to online abuse.
  • Cooperation strengthens the response. Clubs, federations, platforms, media organisations, advocacy groups, and other stakeholders can contribute different forms of support, expertise, and action.
  • Social conditions influence online behaviour. Education, standards, research, policy, technology, and cultural norms can affect how online abuse is understood, enabled, prevented, and challenged.
  • Sport is part of a wider social context. Sporting communities are influenced by wider cultural norms and can also contribute to shaping expectations and behaviour across society.

content.heading: Your heading
content.paragraph_1:
You are part of a wider system. 

Individual actions can reduce harm and support others. Organisations provide the structures that turn those actions into collective responses. Across society, connected efforts in education, policy, technology, research, and community standards can help create safer digital spaces in sport.

UAOA helps connect these levels of action. 

Through Stronger Together, UAOA brings people and organisations across sport together to strengthen how they prepare for, prevent, and respond to online abuse, turning shared knowledge and coordinated action into practical support for the sporting community.
